name: Why antibiotics do not work on viruses
headline: Why antibiotics do not work for colds, flu and most coughs, and what the NHS says instead
summary: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so the NHS says they do not help colds, flu or most coughs and sore throats.
keyPoints: The NHS says antibiotics do not work against viral infections, which include the common cold, flu and most coughs and sore throats.
NHS inform says antibiotics are not often prescribed for mild bacterial infections, because the immune system can usually clear them.
Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can make harmful bacteria resistant, so the medicine may not work when it is needed.
NHS inform says to finish a course even when feeling better, while WHO notes shorter courses may work for some infections, so sources differ in emphasis.
For breathlessness or chest pain the NHS points to a GP, NHS 111 if the practice is closed, and 999 for severe difficulty breathing.

body.heading: What is the difference between bacteria and viruses?
body.body: Antibiotics are medicines that treat infections caused by bacteria. They work by killing bacteria or by stopping them from growing. The NHS says antibiotics do not work against viral infections. That includes the common cold, flu and most coughs and sore throats.

body.heading: When does the NHS say antibiotics are needed?
body.body: In the UK, antibiotics are only available on prescription from a doctor or a dentist. The NHS says they are used for serious bacterial infections, such as sepsis, pneumonia, gonorrhoea and meningococcal meningitis. NHS inform says antibiotics are not often prescribed for mild bacterial infections, because the immune system can usually clear these on its own. NHS 111 Wales says antibiotics are no longer routinely used for chest infections, ear infections in children or sore throats. Amoxicillin, which this site describes on its own page, belongs to a family of antibiotics called the penicillins. A penicillin works only on bacteria, so it has no effect on a cold or flu virus.

body.heading: Why do antibiotics not help colds, flu and coughs?
body.body: All colds and most coughs and sore throats are caused by viruses, according to NHS trust leaflets, which is why antibiotics are not the answer for them. The NHS says the common cold is caused by a virus, so antibiotics are not used to treat it. NHS inform says GPs do not recommend antibiotics for flu, because they will not relieve symptoms or speed up recovery. NICE guidance on acute cough says the illness is usually self-limiting, which means it gets better without antibiotics. Trust leaflets reported in search results add that most coughs and colds get better just as quickly without antibiotics.

body.heading: What is antibiotic resistance?
body.body: Bacteria can adapt so that an antibiotic no longer works against them, which is called antibiotic resistance. NHS inform says taking antibiotics when they are not needed can make harmful bacteria in the body resistant. That means the medicine may not work when it is needed. Trust leaflets also point out that fewer new antibiotics have been discovered in recent years. A UKHSA campaign called Keep Antibiotics Working, as summarised by a local NHS body, says leftover antibiotics are not to be saved, because they may not work properly and may add to resistance. NHS pages say unused antibiotics should go back to a pharmacy rather than be saved or shared.

body.heading: Should an antibiotic course always be finished?
body.body: NHS inform says a course of antibiotics must be finished even when the person feels better. It says that stopping early can let bacteria become resistant to the antibiotic. An NHS trust leaflet frames this as finishing the full prescribed course unless a healthcare professional says otherwise. The WHO has an older commentary that also tells people to complete the full prescription, because stopping early can promote drug-resistant bacteria. The same WHO commentary says evidence is emerging that shorter courses may work for some infections, and that WHO is updating its guidelines on prescribing. Published research reviews also discuss whether advice to complete every course should change, and describe stopping when better as an idea still being studied. So the sources differ in emphasis, and the NHS leaflets point back to the prescriber's instructions for a particular course.

body.heading: What helps with a viral illness?
body.body: Trust leaflets describe the usual advice for colds and coughs as rest and fluids, with over-the-counter remedies if needed. The NHS common cold page says a pharmacist can advise on over-the-counter medicines, and lists paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches or a high temperature. NICE says honey may be used for cough in people older than one year. NICE also says limited evidence suggests antihistamines, decongestants and codeine-containing cough medicines do not help cough symptoms.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to get help urgently?
body.body: The NHS common cold page advises seeing a GP for shortness of breath or chest pain. NHS inform says to contact the GP urgently when someone is more short of breath than usual or is coughing up blood. It adds that NHS 111 can be called when the GP practice is closed. NHS inform says to call 999 for severe difficulty breathing, such as struggling to speak without pausing, gasping or choking. It also lists severe chest pain in the middle of the chest that does not go away, pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw, and feeling more drowsy than usual or finding it harder to wake. After an antibiotic course, a trust leaflet advises contacting a doctor about a high temperature, feeling unwell or symptoms that persist or come back. A trust leaflet lists feeling sick, diarrhoea and bloating as common reactions to antibiotics, and says some people have an allergic reaction with a rash, swelling or difficulty breathing. For urgent advice that cannot wait, NHS 111 is the route, and 999 is for emergencies such as severe difficulty breathing. For non-urgent questions about a medicine, a pharmacist or GP can help.
